--- title: "Dependent data" description: "Visits to one site and neighbouring sites share their water and seabed, so a survey's rows are worth fewer independent stations than their number. Resampling whole sites and whole areas measures the shortfall, and shows which of it a random forest's inputs explain." order: 3 categories: [assumptions, spatial-temporal] --- {{< new-terms >}} ## Rows that share conditions are not separate evidence Two observations are independent when one says nothing about the other beyond what their inputs say. **Dependent data** share conditions, so one does say something about the other. [The coastal survey](../02-marine-data/the-coastal-survey.qmd#repeat-visits-to-the-same-sites-are-not-independent) found that its rows come from far fewer monitoring sites, and called treating repeat visits as separate observations pseudo-replication; that is why [Splitting the data](../02-marine-data/splitting-data.qmd) keeps each site's rows together. Neighbouring sites share a water mass and a stretch of seabed too, and samples from one year share its weather. This page measures what the survey's rows are worth as evidence, and whether a model's inputs take the dependence away. The answer decides how a model must be scored. The same problem appears wherever one unit is sampled several times: | What is repeated | What the rows share | The unit to count | | --- | --- | --- | | Visits to a fixed station | Depth, seabed, local water | The station | | Sub-samples from one grab | The grab | The grab | | Fish measured from one haul | The haul, the gear, the day | The haul | | Readings down one CTD cast | The water column | The cast | ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the data on this page The coastal survey used here is **simulated**, not a real survey. That is deliberate: because we wrote the generating process (`R/make-example-data.R`), we know the true relationships and can show whether a model recovers them. No real survey is being misrepresented, and the figures are not results about any real species. See `data/README.md` for what is built into it. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the Python tabs Most code blocks on this page have an **R** and a **Python** tab, and picking one switches the whole page. Both run when the site is built, and each tab shows its own output. The Python tab is the scikit-learn equivalent of the R; the figures come from R throughout, and a few steps with no scikit-learn counterpart have no Python tab, which is itself worth noticing. Expect the **numbers to differ slightly** where randomness is involved: R and Python draw their random splits from different generators, so the split is not the same one. The conclusions are. ::: ## Resampling whole groups measures the effective sample size A [bootstrap sample](../03-supervised-learning/forests-and-boosting.qmd#a-random-forest-averages-trees-grown-on-resampled-data) draws rows at random with replacement, as many as the data has. Drawing many and computing an average in each shows how far that average moves from one sample of the survey to the next. Drawing single rows treats every row as independent. Drawing whole sites, each with all its visits, treats only the sites as independent, and drawing whole **spatial blocks**, squares of the map with every site in them, treats only the areas as independent. If drawing larger groups spreads the average wider, the rows inside a group were partly repeating each other. The difference converts into a number of stations. An average's spread shrinks with the square root of the number of independent observations, so a spread $k$ times wider means the rows are worth $k^2$ times fewer: the **effective sample size**. ::: {.diagram} ![Visits to one site share its water and seabed. Resampling stations draws single visits, so every row counts as separate evidence. Resampling sites draws a site with all its visits, so only sites count. If resampling sites spreads an estimate wider, the visits were repeating each other.](img/resample-sites.svg){fig-alt="Three cards. The survey, sites with repeat visits: four sites, A to D, each a box holding three to five visits drawn as dots in the site's colour; visits to one site share its water and seabed, so they tend to agree. Resample stations, draw one row at a time: sixteen draws of a single visit each, with the colours mixed, so every row counts as separate evidence. Resample sites, draw whole sites: four draws of a whole site with all its visits, one site drawn twice and one not at all, so only sites count as separate evidence. A note says if resampling sites spreads an estimate wider, the visits were repeating each other."} ::: ## Worked example The whole survey is used, since nothing on this page is a final score. Each site is given a block: the square of half a degree, about 40 by 55 km, that holds the centre of its stations. Five hundred bootstrap samples are drawn by station, by site and by block. ### Preparing the data ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} survey <- load_coastal_survey_clean() |> # the half-degree square holding the centre of each site's stations mutate(block = paste(floor(mean(longitude) / 0.5), floor(mean(latitude) / 0.5)), .by = site_id) resamples <- list( "Single stations" = bootstraps(survey, times = 500), "Whole sites" = group_bootstraps(survey, group = site_id, times = 500), "Whole blocks" = group_bootstraps(survey, group = block, times = 500) ) folds <- group_vfold_cv(survey, group = site_id, v = 10) # how far the average of some values moves from one resample to the next, # for each way of resampling spread_of <- function(values) { map_dbl(resamples, \(r) { sd(map_dbl(r$splits, \(s) mean(values[as.integer(s)]))) }) } tibble(stations = nrow(survey), sites = n_distinct(survey$site_id), blocks = n_distinct(survey$block)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| stations| sites| blocks| |--------:|-----:|------:| | 800| 160| 20|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} import numpy as np import pandas as pd from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestRegressor from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer from sklearn.model_selection import GroupKFold, cross_val_predict from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder from mlbasic_data import load_coastal_survey_clean survey = load_coastal_survey_clean() # the half-degree square holding the centre of each site's stations centre = survey.groupby("site_id")[["longitude", "latitude"]].transform("mean") survey["block"] = (np.floor(centre["longitude"] / 0.5).astype(int).astype(str) + " " + np.floor(centre["latitude"] / 0.5).astype(int).astype(str)) rng = np.random.default_rng(123) levels = {"Single stations": "station_id", "Whole sites": "site_id", "Whole blocks": "block"} def resamples(column, times=500): """Row numbers of each bootstrap sample that draws whole groups.""" rows_of = list(survey.groupby(column).indices.values()) samples = [] for _ in range(times): drawn = rng.integers(0, len(rows_of), len(rows_of)) samples.append(np.concatenate([rows_of[i] for i in drawn])) return samples samples = {level: resamples(column) for level, column in levels.items()} def spread_of(values): values = np.asarray(values) return pd.Series({level: np.std([values[rows].mean() for rows in drawn], ddof=1) for level, drawn in samples.items()}) pd.DataFrame({"stations": [len(survey)], "sites": [survey["site_id"].nunique()], "blocks": [survey["block"].nunique()]}) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | stations | sites | blocks | |-----------:|--------:|---------:| | 800 | 160 | 20 | ::: ::: ::: ### Visits and neighbouring sites repeat each other's catch The first estimate is the simplest: the average catch per station, in each of the bootstrap samples. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} catch_spread <- tibble(resampled = names(resamples), spread = spread_of(survey$abundance)) |> mutate(wider = spread / first(spread), worth = nrow(survey) / wider^2) catch_spread |> mutate(across(spread:wider, \(x) round(x, 2)), worth = round(worth)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|resampled | spread| wider| worth| |:---------------|------:|-----:|-----:| |Single stations | 0.17| 1.00| 800| |Whole sites | 0.22| 1.31| 468| |Whole blocks | 0.40| 2.34| 146|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} catch_spread = spread_of(survey["abundance"]).rename("spread").to_frame() catch_spread["wider"] = catch_spread["spread"] / catch_spread["spread"].iloc[0] catch_spread["worth"] = len(survey) / catch_spread["wider"] ** 2 catch_spread.round({"spread": 2, "wider": 2, "worth": 0}).reset_index( names="resampled") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | resampled | spread | wider | worth | |:----------------|---------:|--------:|--------:| | Single stations | 0.17 | 1 | 800 | | Whole sites | 0.23 | 1.38 | 417 | | Whole blocks | 0.36 | 2.16 | 172 | ::: ::: ::: The 800 stations come from 160 sites in 20 blocks. Drawing whole sites spreads the average catch 1.31 times wider than drawing single stations, so for this estimate the rows are worth about 470 independent stations. Drawing whole blocks spreads it 2.34 times wider, and the rows are worth about 150. An interval for the average built as if all 800 were independent would be too narrow by that factor. A site's depth, temperature and seabed stay the same from one visit to the next, so a deep muddy site is rich every time it is sampled and a shallow rocky one poor every time. Neighbouring sites share those conditions too: the shelf deepens offshore, so a block of the map is shallow or deep as a whole. ### The forest's errors stay linked within a site more than between neighbours A model knows each station's depth, temperature and seabed. Once those are in the model, what is left for rows to share is only what the inputs miss, and that shows in the model's errors. The random forest of [Random forests and boosting](../03-supervised-learning/forests-and-boosting.qmd), 500 trees on six inputs, predicts every station from folds of sites it was not fitted to, as in [Hyperparameter selection](../05-generalisation/hyperparameter-selection.qmd). Its errors, the animals caught minus the number predicted, are then resampled as the catch was. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} forest <- workflow( recipe(abundance ~ depth_m + temperature_c + chlorophyll_mg_m3 + salinity_psu + substrate + season, data = survey) |> step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors()), rand_forest(trees = 500) |> set_engine("ranger", seed = 123) |> set_mode("regression") ) # every station, predicted by a forest that never saw its site predicted <- fit_resamples(forest, folds, control = control_resamples(save_pred = TRUE)) |> collect_predictions() |> arrange(.row) |> pull(.pred) error_spread <- tibble(resampled = names(resamples), spread = spread_of(survey$abundance - predicted)) |> mutate(wider = spread / first(spread), worth = nrow(survey) / wider^2) error_spread |> mutate(across(spread:wider, \(x) round(x, 2)), worth = round(worth)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|resampled | spread| wider| worth| |:---------------|------:|-----:|-----:| |Single stations | 0.16| 1.00| 800| |Whole sites | 0.20| 1.25| 513| |Whole blocks | 0.22| 1.36| 430|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} numeric = ["depth_m", "temperature_c", "chlorophyll_mg_m3", "salinity_psu"] categorical = ["substrate", "season"] predictors = numeric + categorical forest = Pipeline([ ("recipe", ColumnTransformer([ ("numeric", SimpleImputer(strategy="median"), numeric), ("categorical", OneHotEncoder(sparse_output=False), categorical)])), # max_features="sqrt" and min_samples_leaf=5, as ranger does ("model", RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=500, max_features="sqrt", min_samples_leaf=5, random_state=123)), ]) # every station, predicted by a forest that never saw its site predicted = cross_val_predict( forest, survey[predictors], survey["abundance"], groups=survey["site_id"], cv=GroupKFold(n_splits=10, shuffle=True, random_state=123)) error_spread = spread_of(survey["abundance"] - predicted).rename( "spread").to_frame() error_spread["wider"] = error_spread["spread"] / error_spread["spread"].iloc[0] error_spread["worth"] = len(survey) / error_spread["wider"] ** 2 error_spread.round({"spread": 2, "wider": 2, "worth": 0}).reset_index( names="resampled") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | resampled | spread | wider | worth | |:----------------|---------:|--------:|--------:| | Single stations | 0.15 | 1 | 800 | | Whole sites | 0.2 | 1.28 | 485 | | Whole blocks | 0.26 | 1.72 | 271 | ::: ::: ::: ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} bind_rows("Average catch" = catch_spread, "Average forest error" = error_spread, .id = "estimate") |> mutate(resampled = fct_inorder(resampled)) |> ggplot(aes(resampled, wider, colour = estimate, group = estimate)) + geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = "dotted") + geom_line(linewidth = 1) + geom_point(size = 3) + scale_colour_manual(values = c( "Average catch" = ml_palette[["vermilion"]], "Average forest error" = ml_palette[["blue"]])) + scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0.9, NA)) + labs(x = "Resampled by", y = "Times wider than\nresampling stations", colour = NULL) + theme(legend.position = "bottom") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![How much wider the average spreads when whole sites or whole blocks are resampled instead of single stations, for the catch and for the random forest's errors. The errors spread wider for sites almost as much as the catch does, but for blocks far less: the forest's inputs explain most of what neighbouring sites share, and little of what visits to one site share.](dependent-data_files/figure-html/fig-spread-1.png){#fig-spread fig-alt='A line chart with three ways of resampling on the horizontal axis, single stations, whole sites and whole blocks, and how many times wider the average spreads than with single stations on the vertical axis, starting at 1. The average catch, in vermilion, rises to 1.31 for sites and 2.34 for blocks. The forest error, in blue, rises to 1.25 for sites and to 1.36 for blocks.' width=1400} ::: ::: ::: In @fig-spread the forest's errors spread 1.25 times wider when whole sites are drawn, almost as much as the catch did, so even to the model the 800 rows are worth only about 510 independent stations. A site's visits share something its depth, temperature and seabed do not capture. Drawing whole blocks spreads the errors 1.36 times wider, against 2.34 for the catch: much of what neighbouring sites share is their depth and water, and the forest's inputs already hold those. What is left by block, a factor of 1.09 beyond drawing sites, rests on only 20 blocks, and a different set of folds, such as the Python tab's, gives a noticeably different factor. Twenty groups are too few to pin it down, so it cannot be taken as zero. The two answers set how the forest must be scored. A held-out visit is helped by the site's other visits, so the folds must hold out whole sites, as they did here. Some of what neighbours share may remain, and an area of the map can also hold conditions the rest covers thinly, the subject of [Uneven sampling and extrapolation](sampling-and-extrapolation.qmd). So a model that will map areas nobody has surveyed is scored on held-out areas, as [Spatial and temporal cross-validation](../07-validation/spatial-and-temporal-cv.qmd) does. Errors that spread clearly wider by block than by site are a sign of something neighbours share and the inputs miss, such as a front or a sediment type. ## Samples from one year share its conditions Samples close in time resemble each other as samples close in space do: one year's cold winter, or one month's bloom, touches every station sampled then. A model that forecasts must also never be helped by the future. Predicting 2021 from a model fitted to 2022 is not merely optimistic; it can never happen in use, so a forecast is scored only on years after those the model was fitted to. [Spatial and temporal cross-validation](../07-validation/spatial-and-temporal-cv.qmd) builds that split. The survey's six years are too few to resample as groups. ## Resampling needs enough groups and their identifiers Resampling by group works when there are many groups. With 20 blocks the survey is near the lower end; with a handful of transects or vessels the possible resamples are too few to give a reliable spread, and **mixed models**, which fit a separate shift for each group, are the usual route. They are beyond this course. It also needs the identifier. `site_id` survived here because the survey kept it. Real datasets often lose the grab, haul or cast that a row came from when the data are summarised, and once that column is gone the repeats cannot be found. Keep the identifier of the unit sampled at every stage, and report both numbers: how many rows, and how many sites. ## Key points ::: {.key-points} - Visits to one site, neighbouring sites and samples from one year share conditions: they are **dependent data**, and count as less than separate evidence. - Resampling whole sites or whole **spatial blocks** instead of single stations measures the shortfall: a spread $k$ times wider means the rows are worth $k^2$ times fewer, the **effective sample size**. - For the average catch, the 800 stations were worth about 470 by site and 150 by block. - A random forest's errors spread wider by site almost as much as the catch, so it must be scored on held-out sites. By block they spread far less than the catch: its inputs explained most of what neighbouring sites shared. ::: ## Try it yourself 1. Draw the folds again with `set.seed(1)`, then `set.seed(2)`, before `group_vfold_cv()`, and resample the forest's errors each time. How far does the factor between blocks and sites move? 2. Remove `depth_m` and `temperature_c` from the forest's recipe and resample its errors again. How much of what neighbouring sites share do those two inputs explain?
